read.sections.0.text.source: Butuan is a city on the island of Mindanao in the Philippines, close to rivers and the sea. In the 1970s and 1980s, archaeologists studied old wooden boats there, called balangay. The National Museum of the Philippines says the boats were built from planks, joined using a method called lashed-lug. It says they were built between the late 700s and the early 900s. The planks are maritime evidence: people here built boats for travel by water. But they do not record who sailed, what they carried or where they went. A line on a map from Butuan to another island would show a possible link, not a proven trip.
read.sections.0.text.back: Butuan is a city on the island of Mindanao in the Philippines, close to rivers and the sea. In the 1970s and 1980s, archaeologists studied old wooden boats there, called balangay. The National Museum of the Philippines says that the boats were built from planks, joined using a method called lashed-lug. The museum says that the boats were built between the late 700s and the early 900s. The planks are maritime evidence: people here built boats to travel by water. But the planks do not record who sailed, what they carried or where they went. A line on a map from Butuan to another island would show a possible connection, not a proven journey.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Late 700s to early 900s" is "akhir tahun 700-an hingga awal tahun 900-an", keeping the English numbers; "akhir abad ke-8 hingga awal abad ke-10" is the textbook way, used only in the teachers' notes, where the English says centuries.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Butuan is a city in the Philippines. It is near the sea. Archaeologists found old wooden boats there. These boats are called balangay. Each boat was made of long, flat pieces of wood. They were built more than 1,000 years ago. The boats are maritime evidence. They show that people built boats to travel by water. But they do not show who sailed. They do not show where the boats went.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Butuan is a city in the Philippines. It is close to the sea. Archaeologists found old wooden boats there. These boats are called balangay. Each boat was made from long, flat pieces of wood. The boats were built more than 1,000 years ago. The boats are maritime evidence. The boats show that people built boats to travel by water. But the boats do not show who sailed. The boats do not show where they went.

read.sections.1.text.source: The National Museum in Butuan also shows other finds from the area. Many were dug up by treasure hunters in the 1970s. The museum says they point to early trade with China and other parts of Southeast Asia. Another museum article says graves in the wider Butuan and Surigao area held many Chinese wares, or pottery. Many were made in the 900s to 1100s, and some later. These objects were imported: made in one place and brought to another. The pottery and the boats are different finds, often from a different time and context. We can use both to ask about links across the sea. But nobody found the pottery inside a boat.
read.sections.1.text.back: The National Museum in Butuan also displays other finds from the area. Many of them were dug up by treasure hunters in the 1970s. The museum says that these finds point to early trade with China and other areas of Southeast Asia. Another museum article says that graves in the wider Butuan and Surigao area contained many Chinese wares, namely pottery. Many of them were made in the 900s to 1100s, and some later. These objects were imported: made in one place and brought to another place. The pottery and the boats are different finds, often from a different time and context. We can use both to ask about connections across the sea. But nobody found the pottery inside a boat.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: The museum in Butuan has other old things too. Some came from China. They were imported. That means they were made in one place and brought to another. Chinese pottery was found in graves near Butuan. Much of it is from the 900s to the 1100s. Some is later. The pottery and the boats are different finds. Each has its own context and date. We can use both as clues. But nobody found the pottery inside a boat.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: The museum in Butuan also has other old things. Some of them came from China. Those things were imported. That means the things were made in one place and brought to another place. Chinese pottery was found in graves near Butuan. Most of it is from the 900s to the 1100s. Some of it is later. The pottery and the boats are different finds. Each one has its own context and date. We can use both as clues. But nobody found the pottery inside a boat.

read.sections.2.text.source: The second picture is a photo of old balangay planks in the Balangay Shrine Museum in Butuan. It was taken in 2015, more than 1,000 years after the boats were built. Look at the shape of the wood and the round holes along it. The photo supports one claim: people in Butuan built boats from wooden planks. A bigger claim, that people in the region were linked by sea, needs more clues, such as imported objects. The photo alone cannot show the route of this boat. It also cannot tell us if trade was always fair or peaceful.

The picture alone cannot show the route of this boat. The picture also cannot tell us whether trade was always fair or peaceful.

write.example.source: The boat remains show that people in Butuan built wooden boats more than 1,000 years ago. The other objects suggest that people there had contact with China. Chinese pottery was found in graves nearby. These clues are different because they are separate finds. Much of the pottery is later than the boats. We cannot yet say where the boat in the photo went. Another source that could help is a record from a port across the sea.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Many of the imported wares come from graves, and some finds were dug up by treasure hunters. The lesson says so plainly, without detail; keep the focus on objects and dates. Exchange across the sea was not always fair or peaceful, but the lesson makes no claim either way. Never ask learners about their own or their family's journeys by sea, home countries, religion or ethnicity.

educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners make a two-clue claim about links across the sea and name what the evidence cannot show. Evidence move: put the boats' date (late 700s to early 900s) and the imported wares' dates (many 900s–1100s, some 1200s–1300s) in two separate boxes on the board before anyone links them. A sound answer uses two clues for wider contacts without claiming one voyage or one deposit.

educatorNotes.1.source: Misconceptions to address: the planks in the photo are not dated to the same context as every other object, and the wares were not found in a boat. The National Museum's 2022 maritime article mentions Changsha ceramics from Mt Kamhantik in Mulanay (Quezon) and from Laurel (Batangas), not from Butuan; Butuan's own evidence is the Butuan gallery and the grave finds of the wider Agusan del Norte and Surigao del Sur area. Source caveat: published dates for the boats differ. The 2022 article gives the late 8th to early 10th centuries, while UNESCO's 2006 Tentative List entry (submitted by the National Museum) gives the 10th to 13th centuries; that difference is itself a good example of evidence being revised.

Source caveat: the published dates for the boats differ. The 2022 article gives the late 8th to early 10th centuries, while UNESCO's 2006 Tentative List entry (sent in by the National Museum) gives the 10th to 13th centuries; that difference is itself a good example of evidence being revised.
